newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Haider sees Austria govt fall despite bank deal.
newsitem.headline: Haider sees Austria govt fall despite bank deal.

text.p: Far-right opposition leader Joerg Haider said on Sunday Austria's coalition government had made itself a laughing stock abroad over a major bank sell-off and predicted it was only a matter of time before it collapsed.

Haider, in a speech to his Freedom Party conference in Linz, said the Social Democrat-conservative coalition had demonstrated its weakness over the privatisation of the country's most prestigious bank, Creditanstalt-Bankverein, and advised his party workers to prepare for government.
"We need a better government...one the people can trust again," he told some 7,000 cheering supporters.
"It will not be long before the Freedom Party will enter government," said Haider, 46, who has predicted he will take over Social Democrat Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's job by 1998.

In one of his most audacious appeals to date, Haider called on the conservative People's Party of Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel to make its mind up whether it wants to work with his party in the future.
Haider's nationalist Freedom Party came within a few thousand votes of the two main parties in European elections last October, scoring nearly 28 percent of the vote.

The anti-immigration, Euro-sceptic party has already won over a sizeable chunk of Vranitzky's working class support and hopes to persuade conservatives they can only retain real power by joining him in a future coalition government.

The two parties could already command an absolute majority in parliament following a snap election in December 1995. The conservatives publicly acknowledged that the two parties had held a series of meetings ahead of a special parliamentary session next Tuesday over the Creditanstalt privatisation.
But it was now unlikely that Schuessel's party would vote with Haider after hammering out a deal over the bank sale during 11 hours of crisis talks on Saturday.
The conservatives lost the big fight to stop Creditanstalt, long considered its fiefdom, from being sold to Bank Austria, which is indirectly controlled by the Social Democrats.

While Schuessel won key concessions from Vranitzky's Social Democrats, including the eventual privatisation of Bank Austria, the Social Democrats will retain major influence in the banking industry for years.

"The People's Party last night suffered a major political defeat for putting the interests of its party before the economic interests of the country," Green Party leader Christoph Chorherr said. "The coalition crisis was not resolved, it has merely been postponed."
Despite the criticism, Vranitzky said his government was united: "As I said before the talks, there was no need to prepare a funeral dirge or compose a requiem (for the government)."
Liberal Forum party leader Heide Schmidt described the coalition row as "a frightening spectacle" which painted an ugly picture of Austria before the world.
Schmidt said the government parties, which have ruled Austria alone or in coalition since 1945, were unable to stop playing politics with the economy, a theme taken up by Haider.
"The whole world has been laughing at the Creditanstalt sale...The two old parties showed they were not interested in privatising the banking sector but protecting their party posts," Haider said.
He said the carve-up of the economy and major institutions by the two parties since 1945 was finally coming to an end.
